> Abstract:Over the last three decades, ensemble forecasts have become an integral part of forecasting the weather. They provide users with more complete information than single forecasts as they permit to estimate the probability of weather events by representing the sources of uncertainties and accounting for the day-to-day variability of error growth in the atmosphere. This paper presents a novel approach to obtain a weather forecast model for ensemble forecasting with machine-learning. AIFS-CRPS is a variant of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS) developed at ECMWF. Its loss function is based on a proper score, the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). For the loss, the almost fair CRPS is introduced because it approximately removes the bias in the score due to finite ensemble size yet avoids a degeneracy of the fair CRPS. The trained model is stochastic and can generate as many exchangeable members as desired and computationally feasible in inference. For medium-range forecasts AIFS-CRPS outperforms the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) ensemble for the majority of variables and lead times. For subseasonal forecasts, AIFS-CRPS outperforms the IFS ensemble before calibration and is competitive with the IFS ensemble when forecasts are evaluated as anomalies to remove the influence of model biases.

# AIFS Machine Learning data

![](/sites/default/files/2026-05/datastore.jpg?46817)

ECMWF is now running version 2 of its Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS). The AIFS consists of a deterministic model, AIFS Single, and an ensemble model, AIFS ENS.

The deterministic model has been running operationally since 25 February 2025 and was upgraded from AIFS Single v1.1 to AIFS Single v2 on 12 May 2026. Further details can be found on the dedicated [Implementation of AIFS Single v1](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/FCST/Implementation+of+AIFS+Single+v2) page.

The ensemble model has been running operationally since 1 July 2025 and was upgraded from AIFS ENS v1 to AIFS ENS v2 on 12 May 2026. Further details can be found on the dedicated [Implementation of AIFS ENS](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/FCST/Implementation+of+AIFS+ENS+v2) v2 page. 

Use of the AIFS deterministic and ensemble model output is governed by the [Creative Commons CC-4.0-BY licence](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) and also the [ECMWF Terms of Use.](https://apps.ecmwf.int/datasets/licences/general/) This means that the data may be redistributed and used commercially, subject to appropriate [attribution](https://apps.ecmwf.int/datasets/licences/general/). 

Output data are provided in GRIB2 format with WMO units. Tropical cyclone track products, where available, are provided in BUFR format.

## How to access AIFS model data

### Dissemination

Real-time data from the AIFS are available via dissemination.

Users can add these products to their data flows in the [Product Requirements Editor](https://products.ecmwf.int/requirements/) by specifying "class=ai". A list of configurable parameters is provided in [ECMWF's shopping cart tool](https://products.ecmwf.int/shopping-cart/), under GROUP D: AIFS.

Please note:

-   These products are provided with the 'ECMWF' [file naming convention](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DAC/File+naming+convention+and+format+for+real-time+data).
    
-   These products are available according to the following [dissemination schedule](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DAC/Dissemination+schedule).
    
-   These products are available with [Pre-Schedule Delivery](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DAC/Pre-Schedule+Delivery) for eligible users.
    

### Open data

Real-time open data are released as soon as the forecast is produced. 

The data are freely available to the user community. For more information on accessing these products, please see the open data [user documentation](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DAC/ECMWF+open+data%3A+real-time+forecasts+from+IFS+and+AIFS) or visit the [ECMWF Support Portal](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/site/support). Open data from the IFS model are also publicly available; see [https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/datasets/open-data](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/datasets/open-data) for further information.

## **Graphical products**

Graphical products are available as part of the [charts catalogue](https://charts.ecmwf.int/) and the [ecCharts application](https://eccharts.ecmwf.int/). If the products are not found, please reload the page.

As part of the AIFS v2 implementation, ECMWF has stopped producing graphical products from third-party experimental machine-learning models Aurora, FourCastNet, GraphCast and Pangu-Weather.

### Archive data via MARS

Historical AIFS Single and AIFS ENS data are available in ECMWF's Archive and MARS catalogues. Users must be registered for archive access. The AIFS single data exists from February 2024 onwards, while the AIFS Ensemble data exists from July 2025 onwards.

-   AIFS Single data in the [Archive catalogue](https://apps.ecmwf.int/archive-catalogue/?type=fc&class=ai&stream=oper&expver=1)
    
-   AIFS Single data in the [MARS catalogue](https://apps.ecmwf.int/mars-catalogue/?class=ai&stream=oper) (restricted)
    
-   AIFS Ensemble data in the [Archive catalogue](https://apps.ecmwf.int/archive-catalogue/?model=aifs-ens&class=ai&stream=enfo&expver=1)
    
-   AIFS Ensemble data in the [MARS catalogue](https://apps.ecmwf.int/mars-catalogue/?class=ai&stream=enfo) (restricted)
    

# Available Products

## Deterministic and ensemble model

The output of the AIFS deterministic and ensemble model is forecast with 6-hourly time steps out to 15 days initialised from the ECMWF operational analysis. Forecasts are produced four times per day (00/06/12/18UTC).

All forecasts are produced on an approximately 0.25 x 0.25-degree grid ([N320](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/FCST/Gaussian+grid+with+320+latitude+lines+between+pole+and+equator "N320 Reduced Gaussian Grid") grid). Open data for the AIFS is disseminated on a regular 0.25 x 0.25-degree grid.

A full list of available products output by the AIFS Single and Ensemble models is available on the dataset description pages for [AIFS Single](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/datasets/set-ix), [AIFS Single Wave](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/dataset/set-xii), [AIFS Ensemble](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/datasets/set-x) and [AIFS Ensemble Wave](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/forecasts/dataset/set-xiii).

# [](#aifs-ens-v2)AIFS ENS v2

[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-CC--BY--4.0-blue.svg)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) [![Framework](https://img.shields.io/badge/framework-Anemoi-orange)](https://anemoi.readthedocs.io/) ![Task](https://img.shields.io/badge/task-Weather%20Forecasting-green) ![Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/model-GNN%20%2B%20Transformer-purple)

The AIFS is ECMWF's **Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System**. It consists of two data-driven medium-range forecast models:

-   AIFS Single v2 (described on the [following page](https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-single-2.0))
-   AIFS ENS v2 (described here)

**AIFS ENS v2** was implemented on **12 May 2026** and supersedes version [1](https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-ens-1). It is run operationally by ECMWF, generating a 51-member 15-day (6-hourly) global forecast four times per day.

## [](#whats-new-in-v2)What's new in v2

The release of AIFS v2 introduces:

-   A new wave component, including 11 wave variables, marking **ECMWF's first operational data-driven wave forecasts**.
-   The addition of a new snow variable to the existing land component.
-   The addition of tropical cyclone track forecasts.
-   The addition of two variables already present in AIFS Single (vsw and cp), to harmonise the two models.
-   Improved vertical velocities, by changing parameter W from a prognostic to a diagnostic field.
-   An improved representation of the stratosphere, with the addition of pressure level fields at 10hPa.

Architectural changes include:

-   Replacing the afCRPS loss function used in AIFS ENS [v1](https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-ens-1) with a multi-scale loss.
-   Imposing the same variable bounding as is used by the AIFS Single model, improving physical consistency.
-   Revised graph features, utilising more edges in the decoder.
-   An improved training regime, using 1 year of additional training data compared to AIFS ENS [v1](https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-ens-1).

For full details of the changes introduced with this upgrade, see the [implementation page](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/FCST/Implementation+of+AIFS+ENS+v2).

## [](#data-details)Data details

### [](#training-data)Training data

The data used for **pre-training** AIFS ENS v2 remains the same as for the previous model version ([v1](https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-ens-1)):

-   Pre-training was performed on ERA5 data covering the years 1979–2022 over 300,000 training steps.

The data used for **fine-tuning** AIFS Single v2 has been updated:

-   Fine-tuning was performed on 1 year of additional data compared to [AIFS ENS v1](https://huggingface.co/ecmwf/aifs-ens-1).
-   In particular, fine-tuning was performed on ECMWF operational analysis data and IFS 50r1 esuite analysis data, covering the years 2018-2024 over 7,900 training steps.

![AIFS ENS v2 fine-tuning](/ecmwf/aifs-ens-2.0/resolve/main/assets/ens_v2_training.png)

*Note: The IFS 50r1 esuite analysis data used for fine-tuning is not available to users. It consists of prototype data from early versions of IFS Cycle 50r1.*

As in previous versions of AIFS ENS, IFS fields are interpolated from their native O1280 resolution (approximately 0.1°) using MARS default interpolation tools down to N320 (approximately 0.25°) for fine-tuning and initialisation of the model during inference.

### [](#training-procedure)Training Procedure

Key changes to the AIFS ENS v2 training regime include:

-   the introduction of a multi-scale loss
-   the removal of reference field truncation, imposing the same variable bounds used by the AIFS Single model to improve physical consistency
-   the revision of graph features, by using more edges in the decoder together with new edge features.

Full details about the model architecture are detailed in the arXiv preprints [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15832) and [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10868).

#### [](#speeds-sizes-times)Speeds, Sizes, Times

Data parallelism is used for training, with a batch size of 1. One model instance is split across two 120GB GH200 GPUs, with an ensemble instance split across 4 gpus. Training is done using mixed precision (Micikevicius et al. \[2018\]), and the entire process takes about one week, with 32 GPUs in total. The checkpoint size is 2.55GB and as mentioned above, it does not include the optimizer state.

The Anemoi framework provides a complete toolkit to develop data-driven weather models – from data preparation through to inference. The development is primarily driven by a number of European Meterological Organisations but open to contributions from any organisation or any individual. The framework is composed of several packages which target the different components necessary to construct data-driven weather models. To aid development and deployment, each package collects metadata that can be used by the subsequent packages. The framework builds upon on established Python tools including PyTorch, Lighting, Hydra, Zarr, Xarray and earthkit.

## Abstract

Ensemble weather forecasts provide a probabilistic description of the future state of the atmosphere and give users flow-dependent estimates of forecast uncertainty. Here, we introduce AIFS-CRPS, an ensemble variant of the machine-learned Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS) developed at ECMWF. Its loss function is the almost fair Continuous Ranked Probability Score (afCRPS). It is based on a proper score, the CRPS, but approximately removes the bias in the score due to finite ensemble size yet avoids a degeneracy of the fair CRPS. The trained model is stochastic and can generate as many exchangeable members as desired. For medium-range forecasts AIFS-CRPS outperforms the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) ensemble for the majority of variables and lead times. For subseasonal forecasts, AIFS-CRPS outperforms the IFS ensemble before calibration and is competitive with the IFS ensemble when forecasts are evaluated as anomalies to remove the influence of model biases.

## Introduction

Over the last few years, several machine-learned weather prediction models have emerged that show a higher level of skill than traditional physics-based models in a variety of forecast scores.

The first generation of these models produced deterministic predictions and were trained to minimise a mean-squared-error (MSE) loss[1](#ref-CR1 "Pathak, J. et al. FourCastNet: A global data-driven high-resolution weather model using adaptive fourier neural operators. arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.11214 (2022)."),[2](#ref-CR2 "Bi, K. et al. Accurate medium-range global weather forecasting with 3d neural networks. Nat 619, 533–538 (2023)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Lam, R. et al. Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting. Science 382, 1416–1421 (2023)."),[4](#ref-CR4 "Chen, L. et al. FuXi: a cascade machine learning forecasting system for 15-day global weather forecast. npj Clim. Atmos. Sci. 6, 190 (2023)."),[5](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR5 "Lang, S. et al. AIFS – ECMWF’s data-driven forecasting system. arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.01465 (2024)."). The MSE training objective incentivises the smoothing of forecast fields with lead-time and a reduction of forecast activity, to avoid the ’double-penalty’ incurred when forecasting misplaced structures (e.g., refs. [6](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR6 "Hoffman, R. N., Liu, Z., Louis, J.-F. & Grassoti, C. Distortion representation of forecast errors. Monthly Weather Rev. 123, 2758–2770 (1995)."),[7](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR7 "Ebert, E. et al. Progress and challenges in forecast verification. Meteorol. Appl. 20, 130–139 (2013).")). Nevertheless, evaluations demonstrated that these models display surprisingly physical behaviour in classical forecast situations[8](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR8 "Hakim, G. J. & Masanam, S. Dynamical tests of a deep learning weather prediction model. Artif. Intell. Earth Syst. 3, E230090 (2024)."), and provide useful predictions, including of many extreme events[9](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR9 "Ben Bouallègue, Z. et al. The rise of data-driven weather forecasting: A first statistical assessment of machine learning-based weather forecasts in an operational-like context. Bull. Am. Meteorol. Soc. 105, E864–E883 (2024)."). The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) is now producing operational weather predictions using the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS,[5](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR5 "Lang, S. et al. AIFS – ECMWF’s data-driven forecasting system. arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.01465 (2024).")) four times per day.

For the usefulness of a weather forecast, it is important to account for forecast uncertainties. Ensemble forecasts are run to estimate the probability density of the atmospheric state at a future time[10](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR10 "Lewis, J. M. Roots of ensemble forecasting. Monthly Weather Rev. 133, 1865–1885 (2005)."),[11](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR11 "Leutbecher, M. & Palmer, T. N. Ensemble forecasting. J. Comput. Phys. 227, 3515–3539 (2008)."). In physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP), this is achieved via running the forecast model from a range of perturbed initial conditions and by introducing stochastic perturbations into the forecast model itself. The aim is to generate a well-calibrated ensemble. This means that on average, the ensemble standard deviation needs to match the root-mean square error of the ensemble mean (e.g., ref. [12](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR12 "Fortin, V., Abaza, M., Anctil, F. & Turcotte, R. Why should ensemble spread match the RMSE of the ensemble mean? J. Hydrometeorol. 15, 1708–1713 (2014).")), and the predicted probability of an event should accurately reflect the observed probability of it occurring.

For physics-based ensemble simulations with the Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) at ECMWF[13](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR13 "Molteni, F., Buizza, R., Palmer, T. N. & Petroliagis, T. The ECMWF ensemble prediction system: Methodology and validation. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 122, 73–119 (1996)."), initial condition uncertainty is represented via an ensemble of data assimilations[14](#ref-CR14 "Buizza, R., Leutbecher, M. & Isaksen, L. Potential use of an ensemble of analyses in the ECMWF ensemble prediction system. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 134, 2051–2066 (2008)."),[15](#ref-CR15 "Isaksen, L. et al. A 50-member ensemble of data assimilations. ECMWF Newsl. 158, 27–29 (2019).") and singular vector perturbations[11](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR11 "Leutbecher, M. & Palmer, T. N. Ensemble forecasting. J. Comput. Phys. 227, 3515–3539 (2008)."). Perturbations to the initial conditions of the ensemble members are then constructed from both (see ref. [17](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR17 "Lang, S. et al. More accuracy with less precision. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 147, 4358–4370 (2021).") for an up-to-date description of the initial perturbation methodology). Uncertainties associated with the forecast model are represented stochastically[18](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR18 "Leutbecher, M. et al. Stochastic representations of model uncertainties at ECMWF: state of the art and future vision. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 143, 2315–2339 (2017)."),[19](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR19 "Berner, J. et al. Stochastic parameterization: Toward a new view of weather and climate models. Bull. Am. Meteorol. Soc. 98, 565–588 (2017).").

For the first generation of machine-learned weather prediction models, ensemble forecasts were mainly based on an ensemble of MSE trained forecast models[1](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR1 "Pathak, J. et al. FourCastNet: A global data-driven high-resolution weather model using adaptive fourier neural operators. arXiv preprint arXiv:2202.11214 (2022)."),[2](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR2 "Bi, K. et al. Accurate medium-range global weather forecasting with 3d neural networks. Nat 619, 533–538 (2023)."),[20](#ref-CR20 "Bihlo, A. A generative adversarial network approach to (ensemble) weather prediction. Neural Netw. 139, 1–16 (2021)."),[21](#ref-CR21 "Scher, S. & Messori, G. Ensemble methods for neural network-based weather forecasts. J. Adv. Modeling Earth Syst. 13, e2020MS002331 (2021)."),[22](#ref-CR22 "Clare, M. C., Jamil, O. & Morcrette, C. J. Combining distribution-based neural networks to predict weather forecast probabilities. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 147, 4337–4357 (2021)."),[23](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR23 "Weyn, J. A. et al. An ensemble of data-driven weather prediction models for operational sub-seasonal forecasting. arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.15598 (2024)."). The resulting ensemble forecasts tend to have too little ensemble spread.

The second generation of machine-learned weather forecast models are based on probabilistic training. For example[24](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR24 "Kochkov, D. et al. Neural general circulation models for weather and climate. Nature 632, 1060–1066 (2024)."), developed a hybrid model that combined a differentiable solver for atmospheric dynamics with a machine-learned physics module. Denoising diffusion[25](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR25 "Sohl-Dickstein, J., Weiss, E., Maheswaranathan, N. & Ganguli, S. Deep unsupervised learning using nonequilibrium thermodynamics. In Proc. 32nd Int. Conf. Machine Learning, vol. 37 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 2256–2265 (PMLR, 2015)."),[26](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR26 "Karras, T., Aittala, M., Aila, T. & Laine, S. Elucidating the design space of diffusion-based generative models. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, vol. 35, 26565–26577 NIPS, (2022).") has been used successfully to create machine-learned ensemble models that are competitive with physics-based NWP models across a range of probabilistic forecast scores[27](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR27 "Price, I. et al. Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning. Nature 637, 84–90 (2025)."),[28](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR28 "Lang, S. et al. Enter the ensembles. ECMWF Blog 
https://www.ecmwf.int/en/about/media-centre/aifs-blog/2024/enter-ensembles
(ECMWF, 2024)."). Next to providing useful information about forecast uncertainties, these models have more stable statistics than the deterministically trained models, as shown by for example spectra of forecast fields, and do not smooth out small-scale structures with forecast lead time.

At ECMWF, the first approach towards a machine-learned ensemble model is also based on a diffusion approach[28](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR28 "Lang, S. et al. Enter the ensembles. ECMWF Blog 
https://www.ecmwf.int/en/about/media-centre/aifs-blog/2024/enter-ensembles
(ECMWF, 2024).") that achieves competitive ensemble scores when compared to the physics-based 9 km IFS ensemble[29](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR29 "Lang, S., Rodwell, M. & Schepers, D. IFS upgrade brings many improvements and unifies medium-range resolutions. ECMWF Newsl. 176, 21–28 (2023)."). In this work, we take a different approach: we introduce AIFS-CRPS, a machine-learned ensemble forecast model that is based on optimising a probabilistic proper score objective, similar to refs. [30](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR30 "Pacchiardi, L., Adewoyin, R. A., Dueben, P. & Dutta, R. Probabilistic forecasting with generative networks via scoring rule minimization. J. Mach. Learn. Res. 25, 1–64 (2024)."),[31](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR31 "Shokar, I. J. S., Kerswell, R. R. & Haynes, P. H. Stochastic latent transformer: Efficient modeling of stochastically forced zonal jets. J. Adv. Model. Earth Syst. 16, e2023MS004177 (2024).") and [24](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR24 "Kochkov, D. et al. Neural general circulation models for weather and climate. Nature 632, 1060–1066 (2024)."). AIFS-CRPS learns how to represent model uncertainty, through shaping Gaussian noise. Its loss function is based on the CRPS[32](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR32 "Hersbach, H. Decomposition of the continuous ranked probability score for ensemble prediction systems. Weather Forecast. 15, 559 – 570 (2000)."), a univariate proper scoring rule. For training, we use the *almost fair continuous ranked probability score (afCRPS)*, a modification to the *fair continuous ranked probability score (fCRPS)*[33](#ref-CR33 "Ferro, C. A. T., Richardson, D. S. & Weigel, A. P. On the effect of ensemble size on the discrete and continuous ranked probability scores. Meteorol. Appl. 15, 19–24 (2008)."),[34](#ref-CR34 "Ferro, C. A. T. Fair scores for ensemble forecasts. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 140, 1917–1923 (2014)."),[35](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR35 "Leutbecher, M. Ensemble size: How suboptimal is less than infinity? Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 145, 107–128 (2019)."), which approximately removes the bias in the score due to finite ensemble size yet avoids a degeneracy of the fair CRPS (see section 4.2). CRPS is a well-established scoring rule widely used for ensemble verification, hence it is a natural choice as the basis for a loss function. The approach requires only a single model evaluation per forecast step, making it computationally more efficient than diffusion-based methods which typically require multiple denoising steps. In training, proper score optimisation allows for the model to be rolled out over multiple forecast steps.

AIFS-CRPS is a machine-learned ensemble forecast model that is highly skillful across forecast lead times ranging from days to subseasonal predictions. Unlike deterministic machine-learned weather models that are trained to minimise mean-squared error, AIFS-CRPS is trained probabilistically using a proper scoring rule based on the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), enabling it to generate stochastic forecasts that maintain realistic atmospheric variability. The model can produce as many exchangeable ensemble members as required from a single trained model. Each member is generated via independent random perturbations.

In this study, we compare AIFS-CRPS against the operational 9-km IFS ensemble for medium-range forecasts (up to 15 days) and subseasonal forecasts (up to 46 days). For medium-range forecasts, AIFS-CRPS outperforms the physics-based IFS ensemble for the majority of variables. For subseasonal forecasts, AIFS-CRPS demonstrates high forecast skill, matching or exceeding that of the IFS ensemble, including improved predictions of the Madden-Julian Oscillation, despite being trained only on short-range forecasts up to 72 hours.

## Results

### Experiments

We train two AIFS-CRPS versions with different grid configurations: The lower resolution version uses an O96 input grid (approximately 1.0°) and an O48 processor grid (approximately 2.0°, see table [1](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#MOESM1) in [supplementary material](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#MOESM1) for summary on the grids). The higher resolution version has an N320 input grid (approximately 0.25°) and an O96 processor grid. Apart from input and processor resolution, the training set-up of the N320 model differs from the O96 set-up in two ways: we train with two ensemble members instead of four, to reduce computational cost, and we do not yet use a minimum pressure scaling factor (see section 4.2). However, these choices will be revised in future work (see table [3](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#MOESM1) in [supplementary material](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#MOESM1) for a summary of the training settings).

However, the ensemble members of the AIFS-CRPS ensemble maintain maintain variability close to the training distribution throughout the forecast range (compare Fig. [1e–h](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig1)). This is an important property for ensemble forecasts and the representation of extreme events such as intense mesoscale and synoptic-scale weather systems, for example tropical cyclones and extra-tropical storms.

### Subseasonal Evaluation

Although AIFS-CRPS is trained primarily for medium-range ensemble forecasting, it is stable at longer lead times and competitive with state-of-the-art subseasonal forecasts. Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts provide an overview of potential global and regional weather patterns at lead times of two weeks to two months and fill the gap between medium-range weather forecasts and long-range seasonal outlooks[36](#ref-CR36 "Vitart, F. et al. The new vareps-monthly forecasting system: A first step towards seamless prediction. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 134, 1789–1799 (2008)."),[37](#ref-CR37 "White, C. J. et al. Potential applications of subseasonal-to-seasonal (s2s) predictions. Meteorol. Appl. 24, 315–325 (2017)."),[38](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR38 "Vitart, F. & Robertson, A. W. The sub-seasonal to seasonal prediction project (s2s) and the prediction of extreme events. npj Clim. Atmos. Sci. 1, 3 (2018)."). The predictability at S2S timescales is largely determined by atmospheric initial conditions, though there are also important contributions from slowly evolving components of the Earth System, including the oceans, sea-ice, and land-surface properties[39](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR39 "Meehl, G. A. et al. Initialized earth system prediction from subseasonal to decadal timescales. Nat. Rev. Earth Environ. 2, 340–357 (2021).").

The AIFS-CRPS subseasonal reforecast dataset is comprised of 46-day, 8-member ensemble forecasts initialised once per week over the period 2018-2022 for a total of 260 start dates. Here, we assess the performance of the AIFS-CRPS O96 ensemble, which is trained against ERA5 over the period 1979-2017. Initial conditions are from ERA5 data with perturbations derived from the ERA5 ensemble of data assimilations (EDA). To provide context to the subseasonal performance of AIFS-CRPS, we compare against operational IFS reforecasts produced during 2023 for the same period, 2018-2022, which we subset to use the same ensemble size and start dates as AIFS-CRPS. The operational IFS reforecasts were also initialised from ERA5 but with perturbations derived using a combination of the ERA5 EDA and singular vectors. Further information on the performance and configuration of IFS subseasonal reforecasts is available in[40](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR40 "Roberts, C. D., Balmaseda, M. A., Ferranti, L. & Vitart, F. Euro-Atlantic weather regimes and their modulation by tropospheric and stratospheric teleconnection pathways in ECMWF reforecasts. Monthly Weather Rev. 151, 2779–2799 (2023).").

The subseasonal forecast skill of AIFS-CRPS relative to IFS is summarised in Fig. [7](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig7), which shows differences in the fair CRPS (ΔfCRPSS) aggregated over different regions, where ΔfCRPSS is defined such that positive values are indicative of higher skill in AIFS-CRPS relative to IFS. To disentangle the impact of changes in the mean state from changes in the predictability of forecast anomalies, we calculate changes in weekly mean forecast skill in two different ways. Firstly, we calculate ΔfCRPSS from raw weekly means without any post-processing, such that (ΔfCRPSS) includes the influence of differences in systematic model biases (Fig. [7](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig7)a). From this comparison, it is evident that forecast skill is improved in AIFS-CRPS compared to IFS for a range of surface and tropospheric parameters at subseasonal lead times. These differences are particularly evident in the tropics, where they primarily reflect small improvements to the mean state. For example, the mean RMSE of tropical 200 hPa temperatures is ~ 0.1 K lower in AIFS-CRPS than IFS.

We also evaluate ΔfCRPSS calculated from weekly mean anomalies (Fig. [7](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig7)b), where anomalies are defined relative to start-date and lead-time dependent climatologies to minimise the influence of systematic model biases. Unbiased calculation, evaluation, and calibration of ensemble forecast anomalies. Quart J Royal Meteorological Soc 151, e4993 (2025)."). We also increase the sample size of reference climatologies by using reforecast dates in all other years within ± 7 days of the calendar date of the anomaly forecast. For example, forecast anomalies for January 9th 2022 are defined relative to the climatology constructed from all reforecasts initialised on January 2nd, January 9th, January 16th over the period 2018-2021.

It is clear from comparing the ‘raw’ and ‘anomaly-based’ estimates of ΔfCRPSS in Fig. [7](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig7) that a large fraction of the differences in subseasonal forecast performance between AIFS-CRPS and IFS originate from differences in the representation of the mean state. Nevertheless, AIFS-CRPS offers considerable improvements in forecast skill compared to IFS for many surface and tropospheric parameters for lead times of 2-3 weeks. At longer lead times, anomaly-based estimates of forecast skill are very similar in AIFS-CRPS and IFS. We see some degradation in week 6 in the Tropics. In addition, anomaly-based forecast skill in the stratosphere is significantly worse in AIFS-CRPS than IFS. This is consistent with the medium-range evaluation in section 2.3 and the reduced weight given to stratospheric fields in the loss calculation.

Other than setting outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) anomalies to zero, the calculation of our surrogate RMM index follows[43](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR43 "Wheeler, M. C. & Hendon, H. H. Monthly weather Rev. 132, 1917–1932 (2004).") and[44](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR44 "Gottschalck, J. et al. A framework for assessing operational model MJO forecasts: a project of the CLIVAR Madden-Julian Oscillation working group. Bull. Am. Meteorol. Soc. 91, 1247–1258 (2010).") and is the same for all data sources.

Estimates of the MJO skill in AIFS-CRPS and IFS reforecasts are shown in Fig. [8](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig8). Despite the short reforecast period, MJO skill from AIFS-CRPS is consistently higher than IFS for several metrics, including correlations, RMSE of the ensemble mean (Fig. [8](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig8)), and the fair CRPS. In addition, AIFS-CRPS exhibits a remarkably good agreement for MJO indices between the average ensemble spread and RMSE of the ensemble mean all lead times, which is required for reliable MJO forecasts (Fig. [8](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#Fig8)b). The higher correlations and lower RMSE for MJO indices in AIFS-CRPS are not a consequence of an unrealistic representation of MJO amplitude of activity, which might favour deterministic measures of ensemble mean forecast skill. ## Discussion

We show that training a machine-learned weather prediction model with a proper score objective such as the afCRPS can lead to a highly skilful ensemble prediction system. AIFS-CRPS forecast skill is higher than that of the 9 km physics-based IFS medium-range ensemble for most upper-air fields and many surface variables. AIFS-CRPS does not smooth the forecast fields and produces a realistic level of variability, even with long rollouts.

Forecasts of surface parameters are sensitive to spatial resolution, which is consistent with deterministic forecast performance (see ref. [5](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR5 "Lang, S. et al. AIFS – ECMWF’s data-driven forecasting system. arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.01465 (2024).")). At N320 resolution AIFS-CRPS shows higher forecast skill than the IFS ensemble for most surface variables.

First tests for longer time ranges indicate that good skill can emerge from a system that has been trained on short-range forecasts only. Although our analysis of subseasonal predictability is by necessity limited to a relatively short ‘out-of-sample’ reforecast period, the results from AIFS-CRPS are very promising. The MJO results are particularly significant as MJO forecasts from the IFS generally compare very favourably to those from other ensemble prediction systems[45](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR45 "Vitart, F. Madden—Julian Oscillation prediction and teleconnections in the S2S database. Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 143, 2210–2220 (2017)."). If these results generalise to real-time forecasts in an operational context, we expect subseasonal forecasts from AIFS-CRPS to be competitive with, or outperform, those from the best physics-based models.

AIFS-CRPS requires one single model evaluation to produce a 6 h forecast step for one ensemble member. This makes inference computationally cheap: a single member 15 day forecast is created in about one minute for AIFS-CRPS O96 and four minutes for AIFS-CRPS N320 on an NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPU, including the time spent reading the initial state and writing the forecast to disk.

Currently, AIFS-CRPS is over-dispersive for some variables, such as geopotential at 500 hPa, in the early medium-range. This is likely related to the singular vector perturbations, which are added to the initial conditions of the IFS ensemble to improve the reliability of the system. The RMSE of AIFS-CRPS is substantially lower and hence such an inflation is likely not needed. For this study, we decided to use the operational IFS initial conditions because this is currently the most straightforward way to introduce AIFS-CRPS into operations.

So far, the ERA5 reanalysis and operational IFS analysis are used as input and target during training. During inference, the model is initialised with perturbed initial conditions from the IFS ensemble. Within our framework, it is possible to include perturbed initial conditions already during training, which we plan to explore.

An important next step is the assessment of the forecast skill of extreme events. Here, CRPS can have limited sensitivity to tail properties of distributions[46](/articles/s44387-026-00073-7#ref-CR46 "Brehmer, J. R. & Strokorb, K. Why scoring functions cannot assess tail properties. Electron. J. Stat. 13, 4015–4034 (2019).").

AIFS-CRPS currently shows reduced forecast skill in the stratosphere, which we believe is caused by its high sensitivity to the vertical scaling used in the afCRPS objective. Revised loss scalings are under consideration to address this issue.
